expectedText:
EMPLOYEE HANDBOOK (EXCERPT)
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

WELCOME
Welcome to Acme, Inc. This handbook describes the policies that apply to your employment. It is not a contract and does not change your at-will employment status.

AT-WILL EMPLOYMENT
Your employment with Acme, Inc. is at-will, meaning either you or the Company may end the employment relationship at any time, with or without cause or notice.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-29]
  "in the absence of distinguishing features or provisions, or a consideration in addition to the services to be rendered, contracts for life or permanent employment are indefinite hirings terminable at the will of either party."
  — Toussaint v. Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Michigan, 408 Mich. 579 (1980) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2222573/toussaint-v-blue-cross-blue-shield/)
  "Blue Cross had established a company policy to discharge for just cause only ... and thereby had committed itself to discharge him only for just cause ... There were, thus, on this separate basis alone, special circumstances sufficient to overcome the presumptive construction that the contract was terminable at will."
  — Toussaint v. Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Michigan, 408 Mich. 579 (1980) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2222573/toussaint-v-blue-cross-blue-shield/)
  "the disclaimer was contained within a welcoming section of the employee handbook rather than in a separate provision where a reasonable person ought to have noticed it"
  — Lincoln v. Wackenhut Corp., 867 P.2d 701 (Wyo. 1994) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1196517/lincoln-v-wackenhut-corp/)
  Known gap: The general rule stated here is correct as a default, but it is a default, not an absolute: an employer's own policy statements — a handbook provision promising discharge only "for cause," for example — can override it, unless an effective disclaimer preserves at-will status. Whether a disclaimer is effective turns on how conspicuous it is: courts have specifically held that a disclaimer buried inside a handbook's welcoming section, rather than set off in its own prominent provision, can be insufficient. This clause is reused across several documents in this corpus; wherever it appears alongside a separate welcome or introductory section in the same document, that section is worth checking against this exact issue — a disclaimer tucked into a greeting rather than given its own prominent place is a real, checkable structural risk, not just a hypothetical one.

TIMEKEEPING
Federal law requires Acme, Inc. — not the employee directly — to make and keep accurate records of the hours worked by non-exempt employees. In practice, that means non-exempt employees are expected to record their own time accurately, since it's what the company's own recordkeeping duty depends on. If Acme, Inc.'s records are incomplete anyway, an employee may still recover unpaid wages by showing the amount of work performed as a matter of just and reasonable inference — an estimate that still has to be reasonably reliable, not any guess — and Acme, Inc. then has the chance to rebut that estimate with its own evidence.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Every employer subject to any provision of this chapter or of any order issued under this chapter shall make, keep, and preserve such records of the persons employed by him and of the wages, hours, and other conditions and practices of employment maintained by him, and shall preserve such records for such periods of time, and shall make such reports therefrom to the Administrator as he shall prescribe by regulation or order as necessary or appropriate for the enforcement of the provisions of this chapter or the regulations or orders thereunder."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 211(c) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, FLSA recordkeeping duty (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/211)
  "Except as otherwise provided in this section, no employer shall employ any of his employees who in any workweek is engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce ... for a workweek longer than forty hours unless such employee receives compensation for his employment in excess of the hours above specified at a rate not less than one and one-half times the regular rate at which he is employed."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 207(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/207)
  "an employee has carried out his burden if he proves that he has in fact performed work for which he was improperly compensated and if he produces sufficient evidence to show the amount and extent of that work as a matter of just and reasonable inference. The burden then shifts to the employer to come forward with evidence of the precise amount of work performed or with evidence to negative the reasonableness of the inference to be drawn from the employee's evidence."
  — Anderson v. Mt. Clemens Pottery Co., 328 U.S. 680 (1946) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/104318/anderson-v-mt-clemens-pottery-co/)
  "The problem was one of degree, not kind — the methods Plaintiffs used to estimate worktime were simply too unreliable to permit a factfinder to draw a 'just and reasonable inference.'"
  — Mazurek v. Metalcraft of Mayville, Inc., 111 F.4th 748 (7th Cir. 2024) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10495444/richard-mazurek-v-metalcraft-of-mayville-inc/)
  Known gap: The recordkeeping duty quoted below is imposed on the employer by statute, not directly on the employee — an employee's own habit of recording time is how the employer's policy typically satisfies that duty, not a separate statutory obligation in its own right. Separately, the just-and-reasonable-inference doctrine has a real limit: a court can reject an estimate as too unreliable to support that inference at all, rather than simply discounting it, if the estimation method itself was too imprecise.

WORK AUTHORIZATION
Acme, Inc. completes Form I-9 for every employee within three business days of their first day of work and applies the same documentary requirements to every employee, regardless of national origin or citizenship status.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-29]
  "an employer, his or her agent, or anyone acting directly or indirectly in the interest thereof, must within three business days of the hire: (A) Physically examine ... the documentation presented by the individual establishing identity and employment authorization"
  — 8 C.F.R. § 274a.2(b)(1)(ii) (Cornell LII text), Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/8/274a.2)
  "A person's or other entity's request, for purposes of satisfying the requirements of section 1324a(b) of this title, for more or different documents than are required under such section or refusing to honor documents tendered that on their face reasonably appear to be genuine shall be treated as an unfair immigration-related employment practice if made for the purpose or with the intent of discriminating against an individual in violation of paragraph (1)."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(6) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  "an employer "must within three business days of hire … [c]omplete [S]ection 2""
  — Split Rail Fence Co. v. United States, 852 F.3d 1228 (10th Cir. 2017) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4153671/split-rail-fence-co-inc-v-united-states/)
  "The evidence unquestionably shows that the employment practices in this case did not create additional burdens to any class of applicants or constitute differential treatment of authorized aliens and citizens. There could have been no discrimination, and the petition for review must be granted."
  — Robison Fruit Ranch, Inc. v. United States, 154 F.3d 807 (9th Cir. 1998) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/755475/robison-fruit-ranch-inc-petitioner-v-united-states-of-america/)
  "An employer who hires an individual for employment for a duration of less than three business days must comply with paragraphs (b)(1)(ii)(A) and (b)(1)(ii)(B) of this section at the time of the hire."
  — 8 C.F.R. § 274a.2(b)(1)(iii) (Cornell LII text), Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/8/274a.2)
  "Paragraph (1) shall not apply to— (A) a person or other entity that employs three or fewer employees"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, small-employer exception (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  Known gap: This clause's documentary-uniformity claim is grounded in 8 U.S.C. §1324b(a)(6), not §1324a — confirmed directly against the statute's own text, not just a case quoting it, so this is no longer an open miscitation, just a citation this clause's single §1324a reference doesn't fully cover. The separate claim that I-9 forms must be kept apart from personnel files is not in the regulation itself — the full text of 8 C.F.R. §274a.2 was checked directly and contains no mention of personnel files. That instruction comes from USCIS's Handbook for Employers (Form M-274), which is agency guidance, not a codified requirement — a real distinction if the reader is deciding how strictly to treat it. Two further qualifiers, found by reading past the already-quoted fragments of both sources: first, the “three business days” timing itself isn't universal — 8 C.F.R. §274a.2(b)(1)(iii) requires an employer who hires someone for less than three business days to complete verification the same day, not within three business days. Second, and more substantial: 8 U.S.C. §1324b(a)(2)(A) exempts any employer with three or fewer employees from this anti-discrimination protection entirely — the documentary-uniformity claim in this clause's body doesn't apply to the smallest employers at all, a real limit this clause didn't previously disclose.

REASONABLE ACCOMMODATION
If you request a reasonable accommodation, Acme, Inc. will engage with you in good faith to identify one. If Acme, Inc. fails to do so in good faith, that failure can be a basis for liability — but generally only where a reasonable accommodation was actually available and the lack of good faith is what kept it from being identified, not merely because the process itself broke down.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-29]
  "To determine the appropriate reasonable accommodation it may be necessary for the covered entity to initiate an informal, interactive process with the individual with a disability in need of the accommodation."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2(o)(3) (Cornell LII text), Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1630.2)
  "she raised genuine factual disputes on whether the school district participated in good faith in the interactive process required by the ADA."
  — Taylor v. Phoenixville School District, 184 F.3d 296 (3d Cir. 1999) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/765245/katherine-l-taylor-v-phoenixville-school-district/)
  "A party that obstructs or delays the interactive process is not acting in good faith. A party that fails to communicate, by way of initiation or response, may also be acting in bad faith."
  — Bultemeyer v. Fort Wayne Community Schools, 100 F.3d 1281 (7th Cir. 1996) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/729768/robert-e-bultemeyer-v-fort-wayne-community-schools/)
  "To show that an employer failed to participate in the interactive process, a disabled employee must demonstrate: 1) the employer knew about the employee's disability; 2) the employee requested accommodations or assistance for his or her disability; 3) the employer did not make a good faith effort to assist the employee in seeking accommodations; and 4) the employee could have been reasonably accommodated but for the employer's lack of good faith."
  — Taylor v. Phoenixville School District, 184 F.3d 296 (3d Cir. 1999) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/765245/katherine-l-taylor-v-phoenixville-school-district/)
  Known gap: The cited cases require more than a bare failure to engage in good faith: the employee generally still has to show that a reasonable accommodation could have been identified but for the employer's lack of good faith — not that the failure alone is automatically actionable regardless of whether any accommodation was actually possible. An earlier version of this clause stated the rule more broadly than that; it's been corrected to match what the cited cases actually hold.

TECHNOLOGY AND MONITORING
Acme, Inc. may monitor use of its email, network, and computer systems. In one state's case (Pennsylvania), a court held that an employee has no reasonable expectation of privacy in communications made using the company's own systems. This does not extend to a personal, password-protected account — such as personal webmail — even when it is accessed on Acme, Inc.'s equipment; in a different state's case (New Jersey), a court recognized a continuing privacy interest in those.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "we do not find a reasonable expectation of privacy in e-mail communications voluntarily made by an employee to his supervisor over the company e-mail system notwithstanding any assurances that such communications would not be intercepted by management."
  — Smyth v. Pillsbury Co., 914 F. Supp. 97 (E.D. Pa. 1996) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2131293/smyth-v-pillsbury-co/)
  "we find that Stengart had a reasonable expectation of privacy in the e-mails she exchanged with her attorney on Loving Care's laptop. Stengart plainly took steps to protect the privacy of those e-mails and shield them from her employer. She used a personal, password-protected e-mail account instead of her company e-mail address and did not save the account's password on her computer."
  — Stengart v. Loving Care Agency, Inc., 990 A.2d 650 (N.J. 2010) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1483465/stengart-v-loving-care-agency-inc/)
  Known gap: These are two states' court decisions, used here as real evidence that this pattern — no privacy interest in ordinary company-system communications, but a separate privacy interest in a personal account — is a genuine feature of how courts have approached workplace monitoring, not a claim about which state's law actually governs a specific employer. Whether advance written notice of monitoring is itself required before any of this applies also depends on the state — that was not checked here. Privileged communications (attorney-client, as in Stengart itself) may get stronger protection than ordinary personal messages; this clause draws no separate line for those.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
I, Jordan Lee, acknowledge that I have received and reviewed this handbook.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
